steps.body: The BIGGER group is the one pairing cannot empty. Say it with MORE: more stars, more hearts, whichever side holds extras.
steps.narration: The BIGGER group is the one pairing cannot empty. Say it with MORE: more stars, more hearts, whichever side holds extras.

widget.prompt: 4 hearts sit ready. Build the SMALLEST star group that is still bigger.

commonCounts.feedback: Four matches the hearts exactly; bigger needs at least one extra.
Seven is bigger, but not the SMALLEST bigger group — five already wins.

widget.missFeedback: Match the four hearts first, then add exactly one more star.
widget.successFeedback: Five — one more than four is the smallest way to be bigger.

predict.prompt: Three elephants or five mice — which group is bigger?
predict.reveal: Bigger counts members; the size of each member never enters the comparison.

cml.actionGoal: Pair the groups one to one, or place both numbers in the counting song, for kcm bigger group.
invariants: Comparison rests on two facts that never move: pairing one to one leaves the bigger group with leftovers, and a number later in the counting song always names more — which is what kcm bigger group uses.
misconceptions: Judging by how much space a group fills, by the size of the things in it, or by which number was written first.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If one more joined the smaller group, would the pairing come out even?

widget.prompt: There are 8 stars and 7 hearts. Which statement is true?

options.label: More stars
options.feedback: Correct — 8 stars against 7 hearts; pairing one to one leaves stars unmatched.

options.label: They are equal
options.feedback: Equal needs the pairing to come out even; here one side is left holding extras (8 against 7).

options.label: More hearts
options.feedback: Pairing one to one uses every heart with stars to spare, so the hearts are not the larger group.

options.label: You cannot tell
options.feedback: You can always tell — pair the groups one to one and look at which side has leftovers.

widget.prompt: When can your eyes alone compare two groups safely?

options.label: When one group is clearly much bigger than the other
options.feedback: Correct — a big gap is visible at a glance; close contests need pairing or counting.

options.label: Always — eyes never fool us
options.feedback: Spread-out groups look bigger than they are; close comparisons fool the eye easily.

options.label: Never — you must always count
options.feedback: Seven against two needs no count; it is close contests that demand care.

options.label: Only when the groups are equal
options.feedback: Equal groups are exactly the hardest case for eyes alone — the pairing settles it.

widget.prompt: What number comes right after 10? Hop one and tap where you land.

commonLandings.feedback: 10 stops one complete hop too soon. Continue the final 1-unit hop to reach 11.
12 goes one complete hop too far. One hop from 10 lands on 11.

widget.missFeedback: Count 1 on from 10: you land on 11.
widget.successFeedback: 11 — one hop forward, and one hop later in the song always means greater.
widget.lowFeedback: Short of the landing — a single hop forward reaches 11.
widget.highFeedback: Past the landing — right after 10 means one hop, stopping on 11.
